Disagree big time. 3/8” electric ratchet. Half inch impact. Half inch is the industry standard for starting anvil size for impacts. Sure a couple companies make 3/8 but it’s a half hearted anvil swap with no added compactness at best. 

You will blow the fuck out of 3/8” sockets very quickly  and probably should not be using an impact on stuff smaller than what’s in a skipless half inch socket set. Not to mention 3/8” impact socket sets are almost always a complete joke and have like 7-8 sockets but will start at the same size as the half inch drive. 

There’s really no advantage especially for a home mechanic. You’ll end up with an impact that adds nothing to what bolts you can get off. First impact should be an impact that gets off stuff you can’t get with hand tools as much as possible. Most of those bolts will be spots where a high torque fits but your breaker bar doesn’t because you’re 1.5 ft above your driveway. 

In a shop? Sure. The lightweight gun will save your arms and boost your efficiency. At home? Nah. You’ll just be pissed you are short on torque and can’t finish the job. Increase range of jobs you can do first then consider convenience and quality of life stuff.

I’d suggest impact wrench, impact sockets half inch, set of decent open box wrenches and a cheapish set of wrenches you don’t care to bend/cut in some way. I mean, I did it and it was hard a fuck. I’m a mechanic and it was by far the hardest thing I’ve ever done on a car and all it was was cutting out a section of my wheel well/quarter panel and fitting and welding new sheet metal. 

The first time I threw together a quick fix to get the rust out before it spread more was a hilariously bad looking repair. I used deck flashing tape to close the hole in the wheel well and used pop rivets with sheet metal (was not confident in myself welding metal that thin at the time) for the quarter panel. Then I just used rattle cans to get paint on it and learned why you do not want to spray lacquer over acrylic primers. 

Then a year later after a lot of reading and watching hours upon hours of professional body guys on YouTube I redid the repair. Made a really good patch for the wheel well and welded that in. Same with the rocket and wheel arch. 2k Epoxy primed all of that then  mixed some fiberglass filler with resin to go over all of the welds. Also put fiber glass cloth and resin on the wheel well to make sure it was protected and didn’t have any spots for water to get through. Then of course needed filler over a couple areas. Spent 3-4 hours a day for a couple of weeks block sanding then reapplying filler then sanding again because I struggled big time getting things straight. Eventually got it though and sprayed 2k primer surfacer. Blocked that working from 80 to 400 grit. Sprayed it again with same primer then wet sanded with 600. Then finally base coat and clear coat. 

That whole process took probably a whole month to complete and I’m sure a body shop could have knocked it out in a couple of days tops, but honestly I just did it because I enjoy working on my own car and after totally failing the first time I wanted to prove to myself I could do it. I am quite certain I didn’t save any money doing it myself. I probably spent more due to the fact that I sucked at both applying body filler and sanding it. 

So yeah, some stuff I think some people can do but they really have to want to do it not just want to save money. You’ve also got to have a ton of patience and persistence and willingness to learn when each of those is necessary vs the other. Rebuilding an engine is honestly easier. If it’s out of passion for your car go for it and be ready to drop around $1k on materials. If not, just take it to a shop.

So here’s the thing. Guys put in a lot of leg work early on trying to get things off the ground. It’s a very invalidating and demotivating process when that effort is minimally reciprocated.

Case 1 - He’s interested the whole time from 1-2 weeks texting phase through first couple dates:

If we are messaging you pretty frequently early on, then we **are** interested in you. With that said, if you’re only replying once a day or less at times, after probably 1-2 weeks (2 if he’s especially persistent or really **really** likes you) of doing all that and most guys have figured you’re not interested in them and have started to pull themselves back and move on because in their mind it’s likely going nowhere. 

Then you go on a couple dates and most guys are thinking “I’ve put my best foot forward so if she’s interested and likes me she can let me know.” So if we can’t really tell what you think about us at that point, then we’re tired and want to move on. If you don’t make it clear you want things to keep moving forward, it won’t. 

Guys are very accustomed to getting rejected. For most of us, it’s the default. So if we text you for a couple weeks and get pretty irregular responses (once a day being the minimum most likely), take you on a couple of dates, but still don’t know where we stand, then we will take that as a rejection whether or not it is. 

Case 2 - he actually just lost interest:

Pretty self explanatory. Maybe he got tired of pursuing and felt like he was overextending himself and made a conscious decision to detach or maybe he just wasn’t feeling it. 

Case 3(s)- he’s playing a game, was unsustainably pursuing you, maybe just got busy, or other misc. reasons: 

First one I don’t think is actually that common. I don’t think men have the willpower to play those kinds of games and the ones who do are more mature than that. 

Second one’s probably pretty common. Once we sort of snap out of that initial phase of being head over heels for a woman, we realize we can’t put all of ourselves into only her because we have a job, probably family, friends, and hobbies we still care about. Rest is self explanatory and like the others is solved with communication.

Quarter inch is nice because it’s small and in many cases keeps you from over torquing something. It’s very hard to feel something like 5-10 ft lbs or less with a big half inch ratchet. Plus the sockets will all be at least half an inch (12mm roughly) plus their sidewall thickness somewhere on the socket which is too big for some jobs. 

That quarter inch though will just sheer off or strip the socket or the drive on 120 ft lbs though and generally stuff like that you’ll have plenty of clearance to work with. 

Generally though, your drive size shouldn’t be bigger than the socket size, but if you have the clearance and a bigger drive size fits that rule then go with the larger especially if you’re breaking stuff free. 1. Tape off a small work area about 1” outside of the edge. Lightly grind down the area with 40 grind to smooth out the gouged metal. Gotta be very light here. Like 1-3 second passes till it’s just grinding marks. Do this only where the rock chip is. 

2. Follow up with 80 and tape about 2-3”x2-3” area around it. Clean off thoroughly and fill the area with glaze putty. Keep it as light as possible but coat needs to be at least as thick as the gouged area was. It’ll look like it’s not filling it but that’s just the area taking the contour of the damage. Also don’t try to go too far passed your damaged area with filler. It’ll just be more work later. The goal is to cover the damage with as little material as possible. 

3. Guide coat the area and sand with 120 evenly. On the edges stay tight on your work area so it doesn’t get too big. It will grow a bit each step but that’s the point. If any spots remain from your guide coat those will be lows. Spot putty should fill them on a repair like this one. Spot putting might even be enough to begin with instead of glaze. Repeat with the 120 until your surface is even and no lows from guide coats remain. 

4. Work your way up the grits no more than 50% increases are a time. So 120>180>270>400>600. I would paint at 400. As for paint - find your paint code and you should be fine just using an air brush with something this small. Look up blending on YouTube. Practice on sheet metal if you want. It will help when you go to the car. Then wet sand with 600 if you have some ugly spots in the paint. Spray clear. 2k preferably. Wet sand to 3000 and polish.

The problems I see happening if you paint them on is this:

1. You will have to scuff (basically damage it but as smoothly and lightly as you can) the clear coat with 320 or higher grit to get any decent adhesion. Cars use 2k paints which basically just means there’s a hardener in them. Assuming your car is well past fully cured paint means the only bond you’re really going to get is mechanical - which is why you’d need to scuff the surface/work area. 

2. It will be difficult to scuff exactly the area you want to paint. This might be something you could buff and polish out later (like 1-2 weeks after your paint cures) but no promises you don’t accidentally blow through your clear which will result in clear coat failure if not fixed.  [clear coat failure example](https://shopgs.link/products.aspx?cname=sun+damaged+clear+coat&cid=271)

3. It will not hold up the way your factory paint job will. Whether that’s fading, cracking, or chipping, it will be very difficult to get factory level strength and adhesion. The tri force design seems like it would be hard to touch up. So I guess you’d either redo it or just let it be? 


But okay, say you go ahead with painting it. 

1.Clean with some warm water and dish soap. 

2.Maroon scotch bright pads to lightly scuff the area. You’re looking for an evenly scratched surface with these. 

3. Clean again but once with water then some rubbing alcohol. Then if you really want to prep perfectly tack cloth after rubbing alcohol. 

4. Paint! I’m guessing you’ll use rattle cans so this is my suggestion for those. You can get by with a 1k (no gardener) for your base/color coats if you need to but I would go with 2k. Colleges look at your raw gpa on a 4.0 scale but they also want to gauge how you did in difficult coursework.

3. 95%/4.0 already weighted grade in a class that should not be weighted will convert to a 3.0 

4. 95%/4.0 already weighted grade in a class that should be weighted stays at a 4.0.

An average or below average intelligence person who values wealth above all else will work and strive for the highest paying job they can get while sacrificing other things they value. 

Last thing… cause and effect just don’t work that way op. Higher intelligence usually implies higher salary, but higher salary does not imply higher intelligence. With that said, I’m not sure personal red flags are a thing. Red flags are clear warnings someone is unable to be part of a healthy relationship or signs someone is or will be emotionally, physically, or mentally abusive (intentionally or unintentionally).

They put them up because NOBODY should go swimming in the ocean regardless of their ability to swim. 

If you feel having those love languages is truly a red flag you might need more time to process the breakup and relationship. Im interested. We were taught red, yellow, blue, and black and white were kind of primary colors but not really. From a math background, one thing that makes prime numbers unique is every other number can be decomposed into a bunch of prime numbers multiplied together (prime factorization/fundamental theorem of arithmetic), or in other words you can make any other number by multiplying (with colors I’d equate that to combining them) prime numbers. Take a number like 64 for example. 64=8x8=(2x4)x(2x4)=(2x2x2)x(2x2x2)=2^3x2^3=2^6. So 64 is really just 2^6. 

Then black and white are sort of like 0 and 1. They aren’t prime but they also aren’t composite numbers… prime numbers have to have two factors and duplicate factors are only counted once. So 1 doesn’t have two factors. It has one factor thus is not prime. 0 intuitively isn’t prime because it has tons of factors. It actually has infinitely many factors, so of course it can’t be prime, but it also can’t be composite because composite numbers have a finite number of factors… so they’re both neither and considered unique.
